code.title: Bubble, selection and insertion sort: count the swaps on the same input
code.python:
# Bubble: swap neighbours that are out of order; stop when a pass makes no swap.
def bubble(a):
    swaps = 0
    for end in range(len(a) - 1, 0, -1):
        swapped = False
        for i in range(end):
            if a[i] > a[i + 1]:
                a[i], a[i + 1] = a[i + 1], a[i]
                swaps += 1
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:
            break
    return swaps

# Selection: find the smallest of the rest, then one swap per position.
def selection(a):
    swaps = 0
    for i in range(len(a) - 1):
        m = i
        for j in range(i + 1, len(a)):
            if a[j] < a[m]:
                m = j
        if m != i:
            a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
            swaps += 1
    return swaps

# Insertion: shift bigger items one step right, drop the key into the gap.
def insertion(a):
    shifts = 0
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key, j = a[i], i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
            shifts += 1
        a[j + 1] = key
    return shifts

# All three: O(N^2) time in the worst case, O(1) extra space.
data = [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]
print("Input:", data)
a, b, c = data[:], data[:], data[:]
x, y, z = bubble(a), selection(b), insertion(c)
print("Bubble swaps:", x, "->", a)
print("Selection swaps:", y, "->", b)
print("Insertion shifts:", z, "->", c)

followUps:
It is called online because it can sort items one at a time as they arrive, without seeing the rest of the input first.

The part already received is always kept sorted, and each new item is simply slid left into its place. Example: receive 5 → [5]; receive 2 → [2, 5]; receive 4 → [2, 4, 5]. At every moment you hold a fully sorted list of what has come so far. Selection sort cannot do this: it must scan all items to find the smallest before it can place anything.

Cost: placing one new item into K sorted items takes O(K) time in the worst case and O(1) extra space.

Bubble sort makes exactly as many swaps as the array has inversions (pairs that are in the wrong order).

Reason: it only ever swaps two neighbours that are out of order, and such a swap fixes that one pair and changes no other pair's relative order. So each swap removes exactly one inversion, and the sort ends when none are left.

Example: [3, 1, 2] has 2 inversions, (3,1) and (3,2). Bubble sort swaps 3 with 1, then 3 with 2: 2 swaps. A sorted array needs 0 swaps; a reversed array of N items needs the maximum, N(N−1)/2 (10 swaps for N = 5).

Shell sort is insertion sort run several times on items that are a "gap" apart, with the gap shrinking until it is 1.

Plain insertion sort moves an item only one step per shift, so a small value at the far right needs many shifts. With a gap of 4, one shift moves it 4 places. The early passes leave the array nearly sorted, and the final gap-1 pass (ordinary insertion sort) then has very little work.

for (int gap = n / 2; gap > 0; gap /= 2)
    for (int i = gap; i < n; i++) {
        int key = a[i], j = i;
        for (; j >= gap && a[j - gap] > key; j -= gap) a[j] = a[j - gap];
        a[j] = key;
    }

Time depends on the gap list: O(N2) worst case with halving gaps, about O(N1.5) with Knuth's 1, 4, 13, 40… Space is O(1). It is not stable.

code.title: LSD radix sort: one stable counting pass per decimal digit
code.python:
# One stable counting sort on the digit at place exp (1, 10, 100, ...).
def counting_pass(a, exp):
    n = len(a)
    out = [0] * n
    count = [0] * 10
    for x in a:                      # how many of each digit
        count[(x // exp) % 10] += 1
    for d in range(1, 10):           # prefix sums = end positions
        count[d] += count[d - 1]
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):   # right to left keeps it stable
        d = (a[i] // exp) % 10
        count[d] -= 1
        out[count[d]] = a[i]
    a[:] = out

a = [170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]
print("Input:", a)
biggest = max(a)
exp = 1
# Least significant digit first. Time O(d * (N + 10)), space O(N + 10).
while biggest // exp > 0:
    counting_pass(a, exp)
    print("After place " + str(exp) + ":", a)
    exp *= 10

followUps:
The simplest way is to shift every value so that none is negative, sort, and shift back.

Find the minimum, subtract it from every element, radix sort the now non-negative numbers, then add the minimum back. Example: [-5, 3, -1, 2], min = −5 → [0, 8, 4, 7] → sorted [0, 4, 7, 8] → add −5 → [-5, -1, 2, 3]. Use long for the shifted values if max − min can overflow int.

Two other options: split into negatives and non-negatives, sort the negatives by absolute value and reverse them, then join; or, for byte-wise radix on 32-bit ints, flip the sign bit (x ^ 0x80000000) before sorting and flip it back after. All stay O(d·(N + base)).

Because each pass must keep the order that the earlier passes (lower digits) already built; an unstable pass would throw that work away.

After sorting by the ones digit, numbers with the same tens digit are already in the right order among themselves. The tens pass must not disturb that.

Example: [21, 12, 11]. Ones pass → [21, 11, 12]. Tens pass, stable → [11, 12, 21]: 11 stays before 12 because it came first. An unstable tens pass may output [12, 11, 21], which is wrong, and no later pass will repair it.

That is why the counting pass fills the output from right to left using prefix sums.

Radix sort is slower when the number of passes times its per-pass cost is more than the roughly log2N cheap comparisons quick sort needs per element.

  • Small N: for N = 1,000, log2N ≈ 10 in-cache comparisons beats 4 passes that each also clear and scan a 256-slot count array.
  • Long keys: 64-bit numbers need 8 byte passes; strings need one pass per character.
  • Cache misses: each pass scatters items to 256 different places in a second array, while quick sort scans one array in order.
  • Memory: it needs an extra O(N) buffer; quick sort is in place.
  • Custom order: it cannot use a comparator, only keys that split into digits.

It wins for millions of fixed-width integer keys.

code.title: Top-down merge sort with a two-pointer merge
code.python:
# Merge two sorted parts a[lo..mid] and a[mid+1..hi] using a temp buffer.
def merge(a, tmp, lo, mid, hi):
    i, j, k = lo, mid + 1, lo
    while i <= mid and j <= hi:
        if a[i] <= a[j]:              # <= takes the left on ties: stable
            tmp[k] = a[i]; i += 1
        else:
            tmp[k] = a[j]; j += 1
        k += 1
    while i <= mid:
        tmp[k] = a[i]; i += 1; k += 1
    while j <= hi:
        tmp[k] = a[j]; j += 1; k += 1
    a[lo:hi + 1] = tmp[lo:hi + 1]

def merge_sort(a, tmp, lo, hi):
    if lo >= hi:                      # 0 or 1 item is already sorted
        return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    merge_sort(a, tmp, lo, mid)       # sort the left half
    merge_sort(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi)   # sort the right half
    merge(a, tmp, lo, mid, hi)        # join them in O(hi - lo) time

a = [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
print("Input: ", a)
# Time O(N log N) in every case, space O(N) buffer + O(log N) stack.
merge_sort(a, [0] * len(a), 0, len(a) - 1)
print("Sorted:", a)

followUps:
Add one check before merging: if the last item of the left half is not bigger than the first item of the right half, the two halves are already in order, so skip the merge.

mergeSort(a, lo, mid);
mergeSort(a, mid + 1, hi);
if (a[mid] <= a[mid + 1]) return;   // already in order
merge(a, lo, mid, hi);

On sorted input every merge is skipped, so each call does O(1) work. There are about 2N calls in total (N leaves plus N − 1 inner calls), which gives O(N). Example: [1, 2, 3, 4]: 2 ≤ 3, so the top merge is skipped, and so are the two smaller ones.

The worst case stays O(N log N). TimSort goes further and detects whole sorted runs up front.

Bottom-up merge sort uses loops instead of recursion: merge neighbouring blocks of width 1, then width 2, then 4, and so on until one block covers the array.

for (int w = 1; w < n; w *= 2)                 // block width
    for (int lo = 0; lo + w < n; lo += 2 * w)  // each pair of blocks
        merge(a, tmp, lo, lo + w - 1, Math.min(lo + 2 * w - 1, n - 1));

The condition lo + w < n skips a block that has no right partner, and Math.min trims the last block. Example [5, 2, 4, 1]: w = 1 → [2, 5, 1, 4]; w = 2 → [1, 2, 4, 5].

Time is O(N log N): log2N widths, each merging N items. Space is O(N) for the buffer, and no recursion stack.

You sort pieces that fit in memory, save each sorted piece to disk, and then merge all the pieces together while reading only a small part of each one at a time.

  1. Make runs: with 1 GB of RAM, read 1 GB, sort it in memory, write it out. A 1 TB file gives about 1,000 sorted run files.
  2. K-way merge: open all runs, keep a small read buffer for each (for example 1 MB), and put the first item of each run in a min-heap. Repeatedly pop the smallest, write it to the output buffer, and push the next item from the same run.
  3. If there are too many runs to open at once, merge them in groups over several passes.

CPU cost is O(N log N); each heap step is O(log K). The disk is read and written in order, about two full passes over the data.

code.title: Count inversions while merge sorting
code.python:
# Sorts a[lo..hi] and returns how many inversions it contained.
def sort_count(a, tmp, lo, hi):
    if lo >= hi:
        return 0
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    count = sort_count(a, tmp, lo, mid) + sort_count(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi)
    i, j, k = lo, mid + 1, lo
    while i <= mid and j <= hi:
        if a[i] <= a[j]:              # equal values are not inversions
            tmp[k] = a[i]; i += 1
        else:
            tmp[k] = a[j]; j += 1
            count += mid - i + 1      # a[j] beats every item left in the left half
        k += 1
    while i <= mid:
        tmp[k] = a[i]; i += 1; k += 1
    while j <= hi:
        tmp[k] = a[j]; j += 1; k += 1
    a[lo:hi + 1] = tmp[lo:hi + 1]
    return count

a = [5, 3, 2, 4, 1]
print("Input:", a)
# Time O(N log N), space O(N). The count can reach N(N-1)/2.
inv = sort_count(a, [0] * len(a), 0, len(a) - 1)
print("Inversions:", inv)
print("Sorted:", a)

followUps:
The inversion count is exactly the number of swaps bubble sort will make on that array.

Bubble sort only swaps two neighbours that are in the wrong order. Such a swap fixes that one pair and leaves every other pair's order unchanged, so each swap lowers the inversion count by exactly 1, and the sort is finished when the count reaches 0.

Example: [5, 3, 2, 4, 1] has 8 inversions, so bubble sort does 8 swaps. A sorted array has 0 (no swaps); a reversed array has N(N−1)/2, the worst case. The same number is the count of shifts insertion sort makes, which is why both are fast on nearly sorted data.

Walk the array from right to left and, for each value, ask a Fenwick tree how many smaller values have already been seen; those are exactly the smaller items to its right.

  1. Replace each value by its rank 1..M (sort the distinct values), so the tree only needs M slots.
  2. Go from the last index to the first: add sum(rank − 1) to the answer, then record the value with add(rank, 1).
long inv = 0;
for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    inv += bit.sum(rank[i] - 1);   // smaller values to the right
    bit.add(rank[i], 1);
}

Example [3, 1, 2]: 2 → 0, 1 → 0, 3 → 2 smaller seen, total 2. Using rank − 1 keeps equal values out. Time O(N log N), space O(N).

Use merge sort again, but count in a separate two-pointer pass before each merge, because the counting test (a[i] > 2·a[j]) is different from the merging test.

Both halves are sorted, so as i moves right in the left half, the pointer j in the right half only ever moves right too.

int j = mid + 1;
for (int i = lo; i <= mid; i++) {
    while (j <= hi && (long) a[i] > 2L * a[j]) j++;
    count += j - (mid + 1);        // right items that a[i] beats
}
// then do the normal merge of a[lo..mid] and a[mid+1..hi]

Example [1, 3, 2, 3, 1] → 2 pairs: (3, 1) and (3, 1). The long cast stops 2·a[j] from overflowing. Time O(N log N), space O(N).

code.title: Lomuto vs Hoare partition on the same array
code.python:
swaps = 0

def swap(a, i, j):
    global swaps
    a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    swaps += 1

# Lomuto: pivot = last item; a[lo..i-1] is the "smaller than pivot" zone.
def lomuto(a, lo, hi):
    p, i = a[hi], lo
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] < p:
            swap(a, i, j)
            i += 1
    swap(a, i, hi)                  # the pivot lands at its final index i
    return i

# Hoare: two pointers walk inwards and swap items that sit on the wrong side.
def hoare(a, lo, hi):
    p = a[lo + (hi - lo) // 2]      # lower middle pivot avoids endless recursion
    i, j = lo - 1, hi + 1
    while True:
        i += 1
        while a[i] < p:
            i += 1
        j -= 1
        while a[j] > p:
            j -= 1
        if i >= j:
            return j                # a[lo..j] <= p <= a[j+1..hi]
        swap(a, i, j)

# Both run in O(N) time and O(1) space.
data = [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4, 7, 6]
print("Input: ", data)
a = data[:]
swaps = 0
p = lomuto(a, 0, len(a) - 1)
print("Lomuto: " + str(a) + " pivot index " + str(p) + ", swaps " + str(swaps))
b = data[:]
swaps = 0
q = hoare(b, 0, len(b) - 1)
print("Hoare:  " + str(b) + " split after index " + str(q) + ", swaps " + str(swaps))

followUps:
For an interview I would use Lomuto with a random pivot, because it tells you the pivot's final index, and that is exactly what quickselect needs.

After a Lomuto partition the pivot sits at index p for good. If p == k you are done; if p < k continue on the right part, else on the left. Example: looking for sorted index 4 in [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4, 7, 6], Lomuto puts 6 at index 5, so only [0..4] is searched next.

Hoare returns only a split point j, not the pivot's place, so you must loop until the range has one element (k <= j → left, else right). It does fewer swaps and copes better with duplicates, so it is the faster choice in production; with many equal values a 3-way partition is best. Both give expected O(N) time and O(1) space.

A 3-way partition splits the array into three parts in one pass: items smaller than the pivot, items equal to it, and items bigger than it.

Only the "smaller" and "bigger" parts are sorted further; the equal block is already in its final place. This fixes the many-duplicates problem: an array of all-equal values finishes after one O(N) pass instead of taking O(N2).

int lt = lo, i = lo, gt = hi;          // Dutch national flag
while (i <= gt) {
    if (a[i] < p) swap(a, lt++, i++);
    else if (a[i] > p) swap(a, i, gt--);   // do not move i: new item unseen
    else i++;
}

Example [2, 1, 2, 3, 2] with pivot 2 → [1, 2, 2, 2, 3]; the equal block is indexes 1..3 (lt..gt). Time O(N), space O(1).

With the lower-middle pivot, the pivot is a[3] = 5, and the partition returns j = 3 after 2 swaps.

  1. Start i = −1, j = 8. i moves right until an item ≥ 5: stops at index 1 (8). j moves left until an item ≤ 5: stops at index 5 (4). Swap → [3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 8, 7, 6].
  2. i skips 2 and stops at index 3 (5). j stops at index 4 (1). Swap → [3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 8, 7, 6].
  3. i stops at index 4 (5). j stops at index 3 (1). Now i ≥ j, so return j = 3.

Result: [3, 4, 2, 1] (all ≤ 5) and [5, 8, 7, 6] (all ≥ 5). Recurse on [0..3] and [4..7]. Note the pivot 5 is at index 4, not at the returned index 3.

code.title: Quick sort on sorted input: last-element pivot vs median-of-three
code.python:
stats = {"comparisons": 0, "max_depth": 0}

# Index of the middle value among a[x], a[y], a[z].
def median_index(a, x, y, z):
    if (a[x] <= a[y]) == (a[y] <= a[z]):
        return y
    if (a[y] <= a[x]) == (a[x] <= a[z]):
        return x
    return z

def quick_sort(a, lo, hi, median_of_three, depth):
    if lo >= hi:
        return
    stats["max_depth"] = max(stats["max_depth"], depth)
    if median_of_three:                       # move a better pivot to the end
        m = median_index(a, lo, lo + (hi - lo) // 2, hi)
        a[m], a[hi] = a[hi], a[m]
    p, i = a[hi], lo                          # Lomuto partition
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        stats["comparisons"] += 1
        if a[j] < p:
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
            i += 1
    a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]
    quick_sort(a, lo, i - 1, median_of_three, depth + 1)
    quick_sort(a, i + 1, hi, median_of_three, depth + 1)

def run(label, median_of_three):
    n = 100
    a = list(range(1, n + 1))                 # already sorted: the classic bad case
    stats["comparisons"] = 0
    stats["max_depth"] = 0
    quick_sort(a, 0, n - 1, median_of_three, 1)
    print(label + ": comparisons = " + str(stats["comparisons"])
          + ", recursion depth = " + str(stats["max_depth"]))

# Bad pivots: O(N^2) time, O(N) stack. Good pivots: O(N log N) time, O(log N) stack.
print("Input: 1, 2, ..., 100 (already sorted)")
run("Last-element pivot", False)
run("Median-of-three pivot", True)

followUps:
Because it moves less data and uses memory in a cache-friendly way, and for simple values that matters more than the number of comparisons.

  • In place: partitioning scans one array from the ends and swaps inside it. Merge sort copies every element into a buffer and back at each of the log2N levels.
  • Cache: quick sort touches one block of memory in order; merge sort touches two (array and buffer).
  • Tight loop: the inner loop compares against one pivot value held in a register.

Quick sort does about 1.39·N·log2N comparisons on average against about N·log2N for merge sort, so roughly 39% more, but each is very cheap for ints. When a comparison is expensive (strings, objects with comparators), fewer comparisons win, which is one reason Java sorts objects with TimSort.

It is an input built on purpose so that a known, fixed pivot rule picks a terrible pivot every time, forcing quick sort into O(N2).

The simplest case: with "last element as pivot", an already sorted array such as [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] is a killer input, because each partition peels off just one element: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons, N(N−1)/2 in general. For smarter fixed rules like median-of-three, special permutations exist too (McIlroy's "killer adversary" builds one for any deterministic quick sort). In contests, such inputs are used to make solutions that sort int[] time out.

Defences: choose the pivot at random or shuffle first, so no fixed input is bad; or use introsort, which switches to heap sort when the recursion gets too deep and so guarantees O(N log N).

Because partitioning swaps items that are far apart, and such a swap can carry an item over another item with the same key, changing their original order.

Example with Lomuto (pivot = last): [2a, 2b, 1], where 2a and 2b are equal keys. The pivot is 1; nothing is smaller, so the final step swaps the pivot with index 0: [1, 2b, 2a]. Now 2b is before 2a, the opposite of the input. Hoare has the same problem.

For plain ints nobody can see this, which is why libraries use quick sort for primitives. For records it matters. To get a stable result, add the original index as a last tie-breaker (O(N) extra memory), or use a stable sort such as merge sort or TimSort.

code.title: K-th largest: full sort vs quickselect
code.python:
# Returns the value that would be at index target if a were sorted.
def quickselect(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        a[mid], a[hi] = a[hi], a[mid]        # middle item as pivot
        p, i = a[hi], lo
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            if a[j] < p:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
                i += 1
        a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]            # pivot is now at its final index i
        if i == target:
            return a[i]
        if i < target:                       # keep only the side holding target
            lo = i + 1
        else:
            hi = i - 1
    return a[lo]

data = [7, 2, 9, 4, 1, 8, 5]
k = 3
print("Input: " + str(data) + ", k = " + str(k))
# Way 1: sort everything. O(N log N).
ordered = sorted(data)
print("Sorted:", ordered)
print("By sorting:", ordered[len(ordered) - k])
# Way 2: quickselect. Expected O(N) time, O(1) space; the k-th largest is index N - k.
work = data[:]
print("By quickselect:", quickselect(work, len(work) - k))

followUps:
Run quickselect for the k-th largest; when it finishes, the top k elements are simply everything from index N − k to the end.

Partitioning puts the k-th largest at index N − k with all smaller items on its left and all bigger or equal items on its right. So the last k slots hold the top k, in no particular order. Example: [7, 2, 9, 4, 1, 8, 5], k = 3 → after selection the last three slots hold 7, 8, 9 in some order.

Cost: expected O(N) time, O(1) space. If they must be in order, sort just those k: O(N + k log k). The other choice is a min-heap of size k (O(N log k) time, O(k) memory), which is better when the data arrives as a stream or must not be modified.

You can no longer hold all the numbers or rearrange them, so quickselect and sorting are out; keep a min-heap that holds only the k largest numbers seen so far.

PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();   // min-heap
for (int x : stream) {
    if (heap.size() < k) heap.add(x);
    else if (x > heap.peek()) { heap.poll(); heap.add(x); }
}
// heap.peek() is the k-th largest

The heap's top is the smallest of the current top k. A new number that is not bigger than it is dropped after one comparison, which is the common case. Example, k = 2, stream 5, 1, 9, 3: heap {5} → {1, 5} → {5, 9} → 3 is dropped; answer 5.

Memory is O(k) instead of O(N); time is O(N log k), read once, and you can report the answer at any moment.

Each partition, on average, throws away a fixed fraction of the remaining items, so the total work is N plus a smaller piece plus a still smaller piece, which adds up to a constant times N.

Call a pivot "good" if it lands in the middle half of the sorted order (between the 25% and 75% marks). A random pivot is good with probability 1/2. After a good pivot, the part we keep has at most 3N/4 items.

So on average it takes 2 partitions to shrink the range to 3/4 of its size. Total expected work ≤ 2·(N + (3/4)N + (9/16)N + …) = 2·N·4 = 8N, which is O(N).

For N = 1,000 that bound is 8,000 steps, against about 10,000 for N·log2N. Quick sort differs because it must process both sides, so every level costs N. The worst case (always the smallest pivot) is still O(N2).

code.title: Two-key comparator: score high to low, then name A to Z
code.python:
names = ["Ravi", "Anu", "Meera", "Dev", "Bala"]
scores = [90, 85, 90, 70, 85]
print("Input:")
for i in range(len(names)):
    print("  " + names[i] + " " + str(scores[i]))

# Python sorts by a key instead of a compare function.
# A tuple key compares the first part, and the second part only on a tie.
order = list(range(len(names)))

# -score turns "high to low" into normal ascending order; name breaks ties A to Z.
order.sort(key=lambda i: (-scores[i], names[i]))

# For a rule that cannot be written as a key, use functools.cmp_to_key(compare).
# Time O(N log N) comparisons, space O(N) for the order list.
print("Sorted by score (high to low), then name:")
for i in order:
    print("  " + names[i] + " " + str(scores[i]))

followUps:
Turn the numbers into strings and sort them with this rule: a goes before b if the text a + b is bigger than b + a.

Arrays.sort(s, (a, b) -> (b + a).compareTo(a + b));
if (s[0].equals("0")) return "0";        // all zeros
return String.join("", s);

Sorting by value or by plain text order fails: for 3 and 30, "330" beats "303", so 3 must come first even though "30" is the bigger string. The rule tests exactly what matters, the two possible joins. Both joined strings have the same length, so text comparison equals number comparison.

Example: [3, 30, 34, 5, 9] → order 9, 5, 34, 3, 30 → "9534330". Time O(N log N) comparisons, each O(L) for L digits; space O(N·L).

Comparable is the one built-in order a class gives itself; Comparator is a separate object that describes any other order you want.

ComparableComparator
Methoda.compareTo(b)compare(a, b)
Livesinside the classoutside, passed to the sort
How manyone ("natural order")as many as you like

Example: String is Comparable (alphabetical), so Arrays.sort(words) just works. To sort by length instead, pass Comparator.comparingInt(String::length). Use a Comparator when you cannot edit the class, or need several orders (by name, by salary, by date).

Pass a comparator that first compares column 1 in reverse, and only when those are equal compares column 0 in the normal direction.

Arrays.sort(a, (x, y) -> x[1] != y[1]
        ? Integer.compare(y[1], x[1])     // column 1: high to low
        : Integer.compare(x[0], y[0]));   // tie: column 0 low to high

Swapping the arguments (y first) is what reverses the order. Example: [[1, 5], [3, 9], [2, 5]] → [[3, 9], [1, 5], [2, 5]]: 9 comes first, and the two rows with 5 are ordered by column 0.

Do not write y[1] - x[1] (it can overflow), and do not build it with comparingInt(...).reversed().thenComparing(...) without care, because reversed() flips everything before it. Time O(N log N).

code.title: Stable vs unstable: insertion sort and selection sort on records with equal keys

followUps:
Take [2a, 2b, 1], where 2a and 2b have the same key: selection sort outputs [1, 2b, 2a], so the two 2s have changed places.

  1. Pass 1 looks for the smallest item in the whole array: it is 1, at index 2.
  2. It swaps that with index 0, which holds 2a: [1, 2b, 2a]. This long-distance swap lifted 2a over 2b.
  3. Pass 2 looks at [2b, 2a]; 2b is already the smallest (2a is not strictly smaller), so nothing moves.

Final: [1, 2b, 2a]. A stable sort would give [1, 2a, 2b]. The cause is the swap between far-apart positions; insertion sort avoids it by only shifting neighbours and never passing an equal key.

Always end the ORDER BY with a column that is unique, such as the primary key, so that no two rows are ever "equal" in the sort.

If you write ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20 and several rows share the same created_at, the database may return those rows in a different order on each query. A row can then show up on both page 1 and page 2, or on neither.

SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC      -- id breaks every tie
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;

This is the same idea as making any sort stable by adding the original index as the last key. For big tables, prefer keyset paging: remember the last row's (created_at, id) and ask for rows after it, which uses the index and avoids scanning the skipped rows.

Yes, such sorts exist, but they are complicated and slower in practice, so standard libraries do not use them by default.

  • Block merge sorts (WikiSort, GrailSort) are stable, use O(1) extra memory and run in O(N log N) worst case. They merge in place using a small part of the array itself as a buffer.
  • Merge sort with in-place merging by rotations is simple and stable with O(1) extra memory, but costs O(N log2N). C++ std::stable_sort falls back to this when it cannot get a buffer.

The usual choices each give up one property: merge sort and TimSort are stable and O(N log N) but need O(N) extra memory; heap sort is in place and O(N log N) but not stable; insertion sort is stable and in place but O(N2).

code.title: Merge overlapping intervals: sort by start, then one sweep
code.python:
def merge(intervals):
    # sorted() builds a new list; copy each pair so the input is not changed
    iv = sorted([list(x) for x in intervals], key=lambda x: x[0])   # sort by start
    out = []
    for cur in iv:
        if out and cur[0] <= out[-1][1]:
            # overlap: extend the last block; max handles nested intervals
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], cur[1])
        else:
            # gap: start a new block
            out.append(cur)
    return out

intervals = [[1, 3], [8, 10], [2, 6], [15, 18], [9, 12], [4, 5]]
print("Input: ", intervals)
# Time O(N log N) for the sort, O(N) for the sweep; space O(N) for the output.
print("Merged:", merge(intervals))

followUps:
Keep the already-merged, non-overlapping blocks in a sorted structure, and merge each new interval into it as it arrives, instead of re-sorting everything.

A balanced tree keyed by start (Java TreeMap<start, end>) works well. For a new interval, find the blocks it touches, remove them, widen the new interval to cover them, and insert the single fused block.

Example: blocks [1,3] [6,9]. Insert [2,7]: it touches both, so both are removed and [1,9] is stored. Insert [12,14]: touches nothing, stored as is.

Each insert is O(log N) to find neighbours, and every block is removed at most once in its life, so the cost is O(log N) amortised per interval. If answers are only needed at the very end, simply collect everything and do the normal sort-and-sweep once.

Sort by start, sweep while tracking the current merged block, and add the block's length to a total each time the block closes.

  1. Sort intervals by start.
  2. Keep s, e = current block. If the next interval starts after e, add e − s and start a new block; otherwise extend e.
  3. Add the last block after the loop.
long total = 0; int s = iv[0][0], e = iv[0][1];
for (int[] x : iv) {
    if (x[0] > e) { total += e - s; s = x[0]; e = x[1]; }
    else e = Math.max(e, x[1]);
}
total += e - s;

Example: [1,3] [2,6] [8,10] → blocks [1,6] and [8,10] → 5 + 2 = 7. Overlaps are counted once. Time O(N log N), space O(1) after sorting.

Store each block as start → end in the TreeMap; to insert [s, e], keep removing the last block that starts at or before e while it reaches back to s, widening [s, e] each time, then put the result.

Integer k = map.floorKey(e);             // last block starting <= e
while (k != null && map.get(k) >= s) {   // it overlaps [s, e]
    s = Math.min(s, k);
    e = Math.max(e, map.remove(k));
    k = map.floorKey(e);
}
map.put(s, e);

Example: map {1→3, 6→9}, insert [2, 7]. floorKey(7) = 6, its end 9 ≥ 2 → [2, 9]. floorKey(9) = 1, its end 3 ≥ 2 → [1, 9]. No more keys → put 1→9.

Each step is O(log N) and a block is removed only once, so inserts are O(log N) amortised; space O(N).

code.title: Insert an interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list in one pass
code.python:
def insert(iv, add):
    out = []
    s, e = add
    i, n = 0, len(iv)
    # Phase 1: intervals that end before the new one starts are copied unchanged.
    while i < n and iv[i][1] < s:
        out.append(iv[i])
        i += 1
    # Phase 2: every interval that starts at or before e overlaps; absorb it.
    while i < n and iv[i][0] <= e:
        s = min(s, iv[i][0])
        e = max(e, iv[i][1])
        i += 1
    out.append([s, e])               # add the fused interval once
    # Phase 3: the rest start after e; copy them unchanged.
    while i < n:
        out.append(iv[i])
        i += 1
    return out

iv = [[1, 2], [3, 5], [6, 7], [8, 10], [12, 16]]
add = [4, 8]
print("Intervals:", iv)
print("Insert:   ", add)
# Time O(N), space O(N) for the output. No sorting is needed.
print("Result:   ", insert(iv, add))

followUps:
Find every stored block that overlaps the range being removed, delete it, and put back the parts of it that stick out on the left and on the right.

Using half-open ranges [start, end) keeps this clean. To remove [s, e):

  1. For each block [a, b) with a < e and b > s, delete it.
  2. If a < s, re-insert the left piece [a, s).
  3. If b > e, re-insert the right piece [e, b).

Example: blocks [1, 10) and [12, 15); remove [4, 13) → [1, 4) and [13, 15). Removing [4, 6) from [1, 10) alone splits it into [1, 4) and [6, 10).

In a TreeMap, start from floorKey(s) and walk right while starts are below e. Cost: O(log N) plus the number of blocks deleted, so O(log N) amortised.

Find the last block that starts at or before x; x is covered only if that block's end reaches x.

Because the blocks do not overlap and are sorted, no other block can contain x: earlier ones end before this one starts, later ones start after x.

Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> b = map.floorEntry(x);   // start <= x
boolean covered = b != null && b.getValue() >= x;

Example: blocks [1,3] and [6,9]. For x = 7: floor block is [6,9], 9 ≥ 7 → covered. For x = 4: floor block is [1,3], 3 < 4 → not covered. For x = 0: no floor block → not covered.

Time O(log N) per query with a TreeMap, or with binary search on a sorted array of starts if the set does not change.

With half-open intervals [start, end) the end point is not part of the interval, so two intervals that only touch, like [1, 3) and [3, 5), do not overlap.

  • Overlap test: a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end, with strict <. For closed intervals it is <=.
  • In the insert walk: for a conflict check (bookings), skip while iv[i].end <= s and absorb while iv[i].start < e. If you want the smallest set of blocks covering the same points, you may still fuse touching ones, since [1, 3) plus [3, 5) is exactly [1, 5).
  • Length is end − start, with no +1.

Example: a meeting 9–10 and one 10–11 can share a room under half-open rules, but clash under closed rules. Decide the rule before coding and say it aloud.

code.title: Minimum meeting rooms with sorted starts and sorted ends
code.python:
def min_rooms(meetings):
    starts = sorted(m[0] for m in meetings)   # the two lists are sorted separately
    ends = sorted(m[1] for m in meetings)
    rooms = 0
    j = 0                                     # j points at the earliest end not yet used
    for s in starts:
        if s >= ends[j]:
            j += 1                            # a meeting has finished: reuse its room
        else:
            rooms += 1                        # every room is busy: open a new one
    return rooms

meetings = [[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20], [10, 25]]
print("Meetings:", meetings)
# Time O(N log N) for the two sorts, space O(N).
# >= means a meeting ending at 10 frees its room for one starting at 10.
print("Rooms needed:", min_rooms(meetings))

followUps:
It depends on the rule you agree on: if a meeting that ends at 10 frees the room for one that starts at 10, they share a room; if not, they need two.

Meeting times are normally half-open, [start, end), so end == start is not an overlap. In code that is the >= in start >= ends[j] (or heap.peek() <= start). In a sweep over events, it means processing the "end" event before the "start" event at the same time.

Example: [1, 10] and [10, 20]. With >= the answer is 1 room. If the room needs to be empty for a moment (closed intervals), use >, and the answer becomes 2.

Getting this one character wrong is the most common bug here, so state the rule before you code and test it with exactly this two-meeting case.

Sort the meetings by start but remember each one's original position, and keep a min-heap of (end time, room id) for busy rooms so you know which room frees up first.

  1. Build {start, end, originalIndex} and sort by start.
  2. For each meeting: if the heap's earliest end ≤ this start, pop it and reuse that room id; otherwise use a new id.
  3. Save the id at the original index and push (end, id).
for (int[] m : byStart) {               // m = {start, end, index}
    int id = (!busy.isEmpty() && busy.peek()[0] <= m[0])
            ? busy.poll()[1] : rooms++;
    room[m[2]] = id;
    busy.add(new int[]{m[1], id});      // heap ordered by end
}

Example: [0,30] → room 0, [5,10] → room 1, [15,20] → room 1 again. Time O(N log N), space O(N).

Use two heaps: one of free room numbers (smallest first) and one of busy rooms as (end time, room number); process meetings in start order.

The rules (LeetCode 2402): n rooms; a meeting takes the lowest-numbered free room; if none is free it waits for the room that frees earliest and keeps its full length; return the room that hosted the most meetings.

  1. Sort by start. For each meeting, move every busy room with end ≤ start into the free heap.
  2. If a room is free, take the smallest number; it ends at the meeting's own end.
  3. Otherwise pop the earliest (end, room); the meeting runs from end to end + (e − s).
  4. Count per room; ties go to the lower number.

Example, n = 2: [0,10] [1,5] [2,7] [3,4] → [2,7] waits and runs 5–10 in room 1; [3,4] runs 10–11 in room 0; counts 2 and 2 → answer 0. Time O(M log N); use long for end times.

code.title: What TimSort relies on: natural runs, and a stable library sort
code.python:
a = [1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 5, 4, 8, 9, 2]
print("Input:", a)
# Part 1: find "runs" the way TimSort does: stretches that are already
# non-decreasing, or strictly decreasing (those it simply reverses).
i, runs, n = 0, 0, len(a)
while i < n:
    j = i + 1
    down = j < n and a[j] < a[i]
    if down:
        while j < n and a[j] < a[j - 1]:
            j += 1
    else:
        while j < n and a[j] >= a[j - 1]:
            j += 1
    runs += 1
    print("Run " + str(runs) + ": index " + str(i) + ".." + str(j - 1)
          + (" descending" if down else " ascending") + ", length " + str(j - i))
    i = j                                # the next run starts where this one ended
# Finding runs is one O(N) pass; sorted input is a single run, so TimSort is O(N) on it.

# Part 2: Python's sort (TimSort) is stable: equal lengths keep their input order.
words = ["pear", "fig", "apple", "kiwi", "plum", "date"]
print("Words:", " ".join(words))
words.sort(key=len)                      # O(N log N), stable
print("By length (stable):", " ".join(words))

followUps:
A run is a stretch of neighbouring elements that is already in order, which TimSort can use as a ready-made sorted piece.

TimSort scans the array once and looks for two kinds of run: non-decreasing (a ≤ b ≤ c) and strictly decreasing (a > b > c). A decreasing run is reversed in place; it must be strict so that equal items are never swapped, which keeps the sort stable.

Example: [1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 5, 4, 8, 9] has runs 1 2 3 7, 6 5 4 (reversed to 4 5 6) and 8 9.

Runs shorter than "minrun" (a value from 32 to 64) are grown with binary insertion sort. Runs go on a stack and are merged when their sizes get out of balance. Fully sorted or reversed input is one run, so the cost is O(N); the worst case is O(N log N).

Because TimSort runs your comparator and trusts its answers to be consistent, while sorting int[] uses the built-in < on numbers, which cannot be inconsistent.

TimSort's merge step skips ahead in big jumps ("galloping") based on earlier answers. If the comparator contradicts itself, for example says a < b, b < c and c < a, the merge can reach a state that should be impossible. Java detects this and throws IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!. It does not always happen, so the bug can hide on small inputs.

Typical causes: (a, b) -> a - b overflowing (2,000,000,000 − (−2,000,000,000) wraps to a negative number), or never returning 0 for equal items.

Arrays.sort(int[]) takes no comparator at all, so there is nothing to get wrong; a bad comparator there is simply not possible.

Python uses TimSort for both list.sort() and sorted(), for every type of element.

  • Stable: equal items keep their original order, even with reverse=True.
  • Adaptive: O(N) on already sorted or reversed data, O(N log N) worst case, up to N/2 extra slots of memory.
  • Since Python 3.11 the rule for choosing which runs to merge is Powersort, which gives slightly better merge orders; the rest is still TimSort.
  • You pass a key= function, not a comparator. The key is computed once per item, then the keys are compared.

Example: sorted(["pear", "fig", "kiwi"], key=len) → ['fig', 'pear', 'kiwi']; pear stays before kiwi because both have length 4. For several keys use a tuple: key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.name).

code.title: Same greedy, different sort key: keeping the most non-overlapping intervals
code.python:
# Sort by column key (0 = start, 1 = end), then keep every interval
# that starts at or after the end of the last one kept.
def pick(intervals, key):
    iv = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[key])
    kept = []
    last_end = float("-inf")
    for cur in iv:
        if cur[0] >= last_end:           # no clash with what we already kept
            kept.append(cur)
            last_end = cur[1]
    return kept

intervals = [[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5], [6, 7]]
print("Intervals:", intervals)
# Each run is O(N log N) time and O(N) space; only the sort key differs.
by_start = pick(intervals, 0)
by_end = pick(intervals, 1)
# Sorting by start grabs the long [1, 10] first and blocks everything else.
print("Sort by start: kept " + str(len(by_start)) + " -> " + str(by_start))
# Sorting by end always keeps the interval that finishes first: the best choice.
print("Sort by end:   kept " + str(len(by_end)) + " -> " + str(by_end))

followUps:
"Keep as many non-overlapping intervals as possible" (activity selection) is the classic case: taking intervals in start order can give a wrong answer, taking them in end order is always right.

Example: [1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]. Sorted by start, the greedy keeps [1, 10] first, and then both others clash with it: 1 kept. Sorted by end, it keeps [2, 3], then [4, 5], and skips [1, 10]: 2 kept, which is the best possible.

Why end order works: the interval that finishes earliest leaves the most room for everything after it, so swapping it into any best answer never makes that answer worse. An early start says nothing about how long the interval blocks the line. The same rule solves "minimum arrows to burst balloons" and "minimum intervals to remove". Cost: O(N log N).

Compare your fast solution with a slow, obviously correct one on thousands of tiny random inputs, and print the first input where they disagree.

for (int t = 0; t < 10000; t++) {
    int[] a = randomArray(6, -3, 3);       // tiny size, many duplicates
    if (!Arrays.equals(fast(a.clone()), brute(a.clone())))
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));   // a failing case
}

Small sizes (0 to 8 items) and a small value range (−3..3) hit ties, duplicates and negatives often, and a failing case is short enough to trace by hand. The slow version can be the library sort or an O(N2) double loop.

Then run fixed edge cases: empty, one item, all equal, already sorted, reversed, and values near the int limits (to catch a - b overflow). For interval problems add touching intervals like [1,2],[2,3] and nested ones like [1,10],[2,3].

Sorting is not allowed when the original positions carry meaning, and it is too slow when the problem can be solved in one pass or the data never fits in memory at once.

  • Order matters: subarray and "next greater element" problems depend on positions. Sorting [3, 1, 2] destroys the fact that 1 sits between 3 and 2. If you only need the positions back afterwards, sort (value, index) pairs.
  • O(N) is expected: two-sum with a hash set is O(N) against O(N log N); the k-th smallest by quickselect is O(N) on average; values in a small range (ages 0..120) sort by counting in O(N + K).
  • Streams: with numbers arriving forever, keep a heap of size k (O(log k) per item) instead of re-sorting.
  • Only the min or max is needed: one scan is enough.

For N = 107, N·log2N is about 2.3·108 steps against 107 for a linear pass.
